sermon:
## Emptiness and the Long Road Home
*When the famine drives you out and the funerals follow you there*

**Text:** Ruth 1:1-22 · **Supporting:** Judges 21:25 · Deuteronomy 23:3 · Psalm 126:5-6 · Hebrews 11:13

The book opens in a famine, and a famine is the wrong thing to find in Bethlehem. Bethlehem means house of bread. There is no bread in the house of bread. That is not a footnote. That is the diagnosis of an entire age.

**The age that does what is right in its own eyes**
The first verse refuses to let you forget when this happens. "In the days when the judges ruled there was a famine in the land" (Ruth 1:1). The days of the judges are the days the book of Judges ends by naming: "In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). That is the world Elimelech is standing in. A covenant people who kept the language of God and abandoned the obedience of God. And in Deuteronomy God had told them plainly that the land's bread and the land's drought were tied to the land's faithfulness. So the famine is not weather. It is a verdict.

Elimelech's name means my God is king. He carries the right confession in his own name and then makes a decision that says the opposite. He leaves the house of bread and goes to Moab, to the people God had named as outside the assembly, "because they did not meet you with bread and with water on the way, when you came out of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 23:3-4, paraphrased in the law). He goes for bread to the nation that withheld bread. He goes to survive, and the text lets the irony stand without a word.

I know this man. I have been this man. I have left the place of obedience for the place that looked like provision, and I have called it stewardship, and I have called it providing for my family, and I have done it while my God-is-king name sat unused on my own lips.

**Three graves in a foreign field**
What follows is told with a flatness that is its own kind of grief. Elimelech dies. The two sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and then "both Mahlon and Chilion died, so that the woman was left without her two sons and her husband" (Ruth 1:5). Three funerals in five verses. The man went to Moab to keep his family alive. He buried his family in Moab.

Naomi is now what the ancient world had no mercy for, a widow with no sons, in a foreign country, past the age of bearing more. She is the most exposed person the law could imagine. And when she turns toward home and tells her daughters-in-law to go back, she is not being cold. She is being honest about how empty her hands are. "I am too old to have a husband... would you therefore wait till they were grown?" (Ruth 1:12-13). She has nothing to offer them. Nothing. Orpah does the reasonable thing and goes home, and the text does not condemn her for it.

Then Ruth says the thing that has outlived every empire that was standing when she said it. "Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God" (Ruth 1:16). A Moabite woman, with no covenant claim, binds herself to the God who had shut her people out, and she does it not when the God of Israel is impressive but when He looks like three graves and an old woman with empty hands. That is not optimism. That is faith. Like those in Hebrews 11 who "acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth" (Hebrews 11:13), Ruth chooses the unseen God over the seen security of going back.

**Bitter, and not abandoned**
They come home, and the whole town stirs. "Is this Naomi?" And she will not let them keep the name. "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:20-21).

Do not rush to correct her. The text does not. She names God as the author of her bitterness, Shaddai, the Almighty, and she is not being faithless. She is being faithful enough to take her grief to the right address. She does not say chance emptied me. She does not say Moab emptied me. She says the LORD has brought me back empty. She still believes He is running this. She just cannot yet see what He is running it toward.

And here is what she cannot see, written into the last line of the chapter like a hinge. "They came to Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest" (Ruth 1:22). The house of bread has bread again. The empty woman has walked back into the place of harvest at the exact hour the harvest begins. She calls herself Mara in a field about to be full.

This is the hidden hand. No voice from heaven. No miracle splitting the road. Just a famine, three graves, a loyal foreigner, and a calendar that lines up too well to be an accident. The God who is doing nothing visible is doing everything. He is the one who sowed in tears in Moab a harvest He means to reap in joy (Psalm 126:5-6).

We want our redemption to interrupt the field. We want it to come as the thing that stops the famine, raises the dead son, rewrites the funeral. It comes instead as a kinsman waiting in a field she has not entered yet, in a line that runs through her sorrow to a manger in this same town, to the Redeemer born in the house of bread who would call Himself the bread of life. The emptiness Naomi names in chapter one is the room God is making for the redeemer she has not met.

She is right that she is bitter. She is wrong only about being alone.

Bitter, but not abandoned.

## Providence in a Stranger's Field
*The chance that turns out to be the kindness of God*

**Text:** Ruth 2:1-23 · **Supporting:** Leviticus 19:9-10 · Ruth 2:12 · Psalm 36:7 · Proverbs 16:33

Chapter two begins by telling you the answer before Ruth knows the question. "Now Naomi had a relative of her husband's, a worthy man of the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz" (Ruth 2:1). The narrator hands you the redeemer in verse one. Ruth will spend the whole chapter not knowing he exists, and you will spend the whole chapter watching God walk her toward him by a road that looks like luck.

**Two widows and the law of leftovers**
Ruth does not wait to be rescued. She goes to work. "Let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain" (Ruth 2:2). Gleaning was Israel's law for the destitute. "When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge... you shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner" (Leviticus 19:9-10). It was God's welfare written into the corners of the field, not a handout from a bin, but the right to follow the harvesters and pick up what they left and what they dropped. It was hard, bent-over, all-day labor for whatever the reapers were not careful enough to keep.

And a Moabite woman is the most vulnerable person to attempt it. A foreigner, in another man's field, among working men, with no husband and no protection. Ruth knows the danger. The whole chapter keeps circling back to it. She goes anyway, because two widows do not eat unless she does.

Then comes the verse the entire book turns on, and it turns on a word so small you could miss it. "She happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz" (Ruth 2:3). She happened to. By chance. The Hebrew is almost a shrug, her chance chanced upon it. And the narrator says it deadpan, on purpose, because you already know what Ruth does not. There is no part of this field that belongs to chance. "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). The accident is the appointment. The luck is the Lord.

**The worthy man who had been listening**
Boaz arrives and the first words out of his mouth are a blessing. "The LORD be with you," he says to the reapers, and they bless him back (Ruth 2:4). That is who this man is before he does a single thing for Ruth. He runs his field as a worshiper.

He sees her, asks who she is, and then does what the law did not require and the culture did not expect. He tells her not to glean anywhere else. He tells the young men not to touch her. He gives her access to the water the workers drew. And when she falls on her face and asks why, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner?" (Ruth 2:10), Boaz answers that he has heard everything. "All that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband has been fully told to me" (Ruth 2:11). Her loyalty had gone ahead of her into the field. The kindness she had spent on Naomi in the dark was being repaid by a man she had never met.

Then he says the line that names what is really happening over this whole book. "The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge" (Ruth 2:12). Under whose wings. The same Hebrew word, kanaph, is wing and it is the corner of a garment. Boaz is praying that God would cover Ruth with His wings, and by the end of the next chapter, Boaz himself will be asked to spread the corner of his garment over her. He is praying a prayer that he will become the answer to. He just does not know it yet. Neither does she.

This is the image David would later sing back to this God: "How precious is your steadfast love, O God. The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings" (Psalm 36:7). Ruth, the foreigner the law had shut out, comes and takes refuge under those wings, and God does not turn her away. He sends her to lunch.

**No such thing as chance**
Boaz feeds her at his own table until she is full and has leftovers to carry home. He tells his men to pull grain out of the bundles and leave it for her on purpose. She gleans an ephah of barley, far more than a day's work should yield, and brings it back to a stunned Naomi, who hears one name and comes alive. "Blessed be he by the LORD, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead... The man is a close relative of ours, one of our redeemers" (Ruth 2:20). The widow who called herself Mara hears the word redeemer and the bitterness cracks. God's kindness, she says, has not forsaken us. The hidden hand is becoming visible to the one woman who thought she had been emptied.

Now turn the mirror. We are far more pious about the bad days than the ordinary ones. We will fall to our knees over the famine and the funeral. We will name God as Almighty in our bitterness, the way Naomi did. And then we walk into the field on a normal Tuesday, and the door opens, and the right man is in the right field, and we call it a coincidence. We reserve providence for the catastrophe and hand the ordinary day to chance. But the book of Ruth has no miracle in it. None. Not one sea splits, not one fire falls. The whole rescue is built out of a famine, a calendar, a relative, and a woman who happened to turn down the right row. God is most at work in this book precisely where He looks least involved.

That is the field we live in. The Redeemer who covers the foreigner with His wings did not come as a sea splitting either. He came as a baby in a field town, in a line that this chance-that-was-no-chance was quietly building. Boaz feeding a foreigner he had no obligation to feed is the small picture of the God who would gather the outsider and the widow to a table and tell them to eat until they are full.

There are no accidents in your field.

No such thing as chance.

## The Risk at the Threshing Floor
*Empty hands, a redeemer's garment, and the courage to ask*

**Text:** Ruth 3:1-18 · **Supporting:** Ruth 2:12 · Ezekiel 16:8 · Leviticus 25:25 · Ruth 3:11

Naomi has a plan, and the plan is dangerous. "My daughter, should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?" (Ruth 3:1). The bitter woman of chapter one is now thinking about somebody else's future. Grace does that. It turns the rescued into the ones who go seeking rest for someone else. But the rest she seeks for Ruth runs straight through a threshing floor at midnight, and there is no safe way to do what she is about to ask.

**A plan that could destroy her**
The instructions are precise and they are perilous. Wash, anoint yourself, put on your cloak, go down to the threshing floor at night, but do not let Boaz know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking. "When he lies down, observe the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do" (Ruth 3:4). A young foreign widow, alone, in the dark, at the feet of a sleeping man at the end of a harvest feast. One word twisted, one motive misread, and Ruth is not a redeemed woman. She is a ruined one. Everything the law of gleaning was meant to protect her from is what she walks into on purpose.

And she does it. "All that you say I will do" (Ruth 3:5). The same obedience she gave to Naomi's God on the road from Moab she now gives to Naomi's plan in the dark. She lays her entire future on the integrity of one man, with no guarantee that he will be what she is betting he is.

**The request that covers her**
Boaz wakes at midnight, startled, and finds a woman at his feet. "Who are you?" And Ruth answers with the boldest sentence in the book. "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer" (Ruth 3:9).

Hear what she has done. Back in chapter two, Boaz prayed that God would reward her, "under whose wings you have come to take refuge" (Ruth 2:12). Now Ruth takes his own prayer and hands it back to him as a request. You asked God to cover me with His wings. Be the wing. Spread the corner of your garment over me. It is the same word, kanaph, the wing of God and the edge of a man's robe, and Ruth uses it to say: stop praying that someone will redeem me and redeem me. It is the exact gesture God uses for His own covenant with His people: "I spread the corner of my garment over you and covered your nakedness... and you became mine" (Ezekiel 16:8). She is asking Boaz to do what God does, to take the exposed, the foreign, the destitute, and cover her and call her his own.

And notice that she comes with nothing. She does not come with a dowry. She does not come with a claim. She does not come having earned him. She is a Moabite widow with an ephah of borrowed barley to her name, asking a worthy man to pay for a future she cannot buy. This is redemption sought the only way redemption is ever truly sought, with empty hands held open.

**The man who guards what he could have taken**
Now watch the integrity of Boaz, because a lesser man would have failed every test of this night. He could have taken advantage. He does the opposite. He blesses her. "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. You have made this last kindness greater than the first in that you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich" (Ruth 3:10). He calls her seeking him an act of loyalty, not desperation, kindness, hesed, the covenant word. He honors her instead of using her. "Do not fear, I will do for you all that you ask, for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman" (Ruth 3:11). She had called him a worthy man back in chapter two; the whole town, he says, calls her a worthy woman. The redeemer and the one he redeems are named by the same honor.

Then he is honest about the one obstacle. "There is a redeemer nearer than I" (Ruth 3:12). The law of redemption ran by blood order, "if your brother becomes poor and sells part of his property, then his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold" (Leviticus 25:25). Boaz will not cut the line to get what he wants. He guards the law as carefully as he guards her purity. He sends her home before dawn so no one can slander her, fills her cloak with six measures of barley so she does not return to Naomi empty-handed, and pledges, "the man will not rest but will settle the matter today" (Ruth 3:18).

Here is the mirror, and it is for the religious among us most of all. We are far more comfortable earning than asking. We would rather glean for a redeemer than lie down at his feet and request him, because gleaning leaves us our dignity and asking leaves us exposed. We want to come to God with a full cloak, with our record, our service, our worthiness, and we resent that the only posture that works is empty hands and an uncovered request: spread your wings over me, for I cannot cover myself. Ruth at the threshing floor is the gospel posture before the gospel had a name. Not the strong negotiating terms. The destitute asking to be covered.

And the man she asks is the picture of the One who came to answer. A redeemer with the right and the willingness, who could have used the exposed and chose to honor her, who guarded the law instead of breaking it to grab the prize, who would not rest until the price was settled. That is Boaz at midnight. It is also Christ, who covers the nakedness of those who come to Him with nothing, and will not rest until it is finished.

She came in the dark with empty hands. She went home covered.

Redemption sought with empty hands.

## The Price Paid at the Gate
*Redemption in daylight, before witnesses, paid in full*

**Text:** Ruth 4:1-12 · **Supporting:** Leviticus 25:25 · Deuteronomy 25:5-6 · Ruth 3:18 · Galatians 4:4-5

Chapter three happened at midnight on a threshing floor. Chapter four happens at noon at the city gate. The book moves the whole question of redemption out of the dark and into the most public place in the town, because real redemption is never a private feeling. It is a transaction, with witnesses, and a price.

**The seat of decisions**
"Now Boaz had gone up to the gate and sat down there" (Ruth 4:1). The gate of an ancient city was the courthouse, the council, the place where deals were sealed and disputes were judged in the open. Boaz had said he would not rest until the matter was settled that day, and here he is, settling it. The nearer redeemer comes by, the man with the prior claim, the one obstacle standing between Ruth and rest, and Boaz calls him over, gathers ten elders as witnesses, and lays it out.

Watch how he frames it, because the framing is shrewd and it is honest at the same time. He starts with the land. "Naomi... is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech. So I thought I would tell you... If you will redeem it, redeem it" (Ruth 4:3-4). The land of redemption ran by the law: "if your brother becomes poor and sells part of his property, then his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem" (Leviticus 25:25). The nearer kinsman hears land, hears asset, hears an estate that increases his own holdings, and he says yes immediately. "I will redeem it."

**The clause that changes everything**
Then Boaz adds the part that was never going to be on the man's books. "The day you buy the field from the hand of Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead, in order to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance" (Ruth 4:5).

There it is. Redemption was never just the field. It was the widow. It was the law of the dead man's name, "if brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no son... her husband's brother shall take her... and the first son whom she bears shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, that his name may not be blotted out of Israel" (Deuteronomy 25:5-6). To redeem the land you had to take the woman, and the first son you raised up would not carry your name. He would carry the name of a dead man. You would pay the full price and the inheritance would be charged to someone else's account.

And the nearer kinsman does the math out loud. "Then I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it" (Ruth 4:6). He is not a villain. He is just a man who will redeem what increases him and refuse what costs him. He wanted the asset without the obligation. He wanted the field without the widow. He wanted redemption that paid him, not redemption that emptied him. And the moment redemption required loss, his right of redemption was for sale, and he sold it.

He is the warning sitting at the gate. He is so close. He is the nearer kinsman. He has the right. He says the word redeem with his own mouth, twice. And he walks away unnamed. The text never tells us his name. The man who would not pay the cost is remembered in Scripture as no one, while the man who paid it is remembered forever.

**Love that pays the cost**
So Boaz takes the right that the other man dropped, and he takes it in full view. He pulls off the sandal, the old custom of transfer, and he declares to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses this day that I have bought from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech and... Mahlon and Chilion. Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have bought to be my wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance, that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his native place" (Ruth 4:9-10).

Hear the verb. I have bought. Twice. Redemption is purchase. Boaz pays the full price knowing the first son will not carry his name. He takes on the debt, the field, the foreign widow, and the obligation to raise up another man's name and another man's line, and he does it gladly, in daylight, on the record. The nearer kinsman asked what redemption would cost him and refused. Boaz knew exactly what it would cost him and signed his name to it. That is the difference between a man who has a right and a man who has love. The right was available to two men. Only one was willing to pay.

And the people at the gate, who watched the whole thing, bless the marriage with names that ring forward through the rest of the story. "May you act worthily in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem" (Ruth 4:11). Ephrathah. Bethlehem. The town where, generations later, a far greater Redeemer would be born to pay a far greater price.

Now the mirror, and it does not let any of us off. We are all, every one of us, the nearer kinsman before we are anything else. We will gladly take the redemption that adds to us, the forgiveness that costs nothing, the grace that leaves our inheritance intact, the salvation with no obligation attached. And the moment redeeming requires that we lose something, the field with the widow attached, the faith with the cost attached, the love that pays instead of profits, we discover how fast our right of redemption goes up for sale. We want a Redeemer who increases us. We were saved by a Redeemer who emptied Himself.

"When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law" (Galatians 4:4-5). That is Boaz at the gate, written large. A Redeemer who had the right and chose the cost, who bought in full what increased Him nothing, who took a foreign and destitute bride to perpetuate a name that was not His own gain but our salvation, who paid the price out loud, before witnesses, in daylight. The nearer kinsman keeps his inheritance and loses his name. Boaz pays everything and gains a place in the line of David and of Christ.

The man who would not pay is forgotten. The man who paid is named in the genealogy of the King.

Love that pays the cost.

## From Empty Hands to the House of David
*The hidden hand revealed, and the king it was writing all along*

**Text:** Ruth 4:13-22 · **Supporting:** Ruth 1:21 · Ruth 4:15 · 1 Samuel 16:1 · Matthew 1:5-6

The whole book has been waiting on one short verse, and when it comes it is almost too quiet for the weight it carries. "So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son" (Ruth 4:13). The LORD gave. After four chapters with no miracle, no voice, no fire, the narrator finally names God as the direct cause of something, and it is the most ordinary thing in the world. A married woman conceives a child. That is where the hidden hand finally shows itself. Not in a sea splitting. In a baby.

**The emptiness filled**
Go back to chapter one and stand with Naomi as she comes home. "I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty... the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me" (Ruth 1:21). Empty. That was her word for herself. No husband, no sons, no future, a name for herself, Mara, bitter, that she would not let the town take from her.

Now hear the women of Bethlehem at the end of the book. "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel. He shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him" (Ruth 4:14-15).

Look at what God undoes, line by line. She said the LORD emptied her. The women say the LORD has not left her without a redeemer. She said she had no sons. They say her daughter-in-law is worth more than seven sons, and in a world where seven sons was the picture of total blessing, that is not a polite compliment, it is a verdict on what loyalty is worth against blood. She named herself bitter. "Then Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse" (Ruth 4:16). The empty arms of chapter one hold a child in chapter four. The God who looked absent the whole way through was filling the very emptiness she had named to His face.

And notice what the women call the baby. They call him Naomi's redeemer. "A son has been born to Naomi" (Ruth 4:17). The hidden hand does not just fill her arms. It writes her back into the line she thought had died in Moab with her sons.

**The name that opens the future**
Then the women do the naming, and Scripture lets the town women name the child who matters more than they know. "They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David" (Ruth 4:17).

There it is. The whole book detonates in one sentence. This is not a sweet rural story about a kind widow and a generous farmer. This is the secret origin of the throne of Israel. The famine, the three graves, the loyal Moabite, the chance that was no chance in the field, the midnight risk, the sandal pulled off at the gate, all of it was God quietly assembling the great-grandmother of David. "The LORD said to Samuel... I have provided for myself a king among his sons," he tells Samuel of Jesse the Bethlehemite (1 Samuel 16:1). That king is David. And David exists because a Moabite widow said where you go I will go, and a worthy man paid the full price at the gate.

The genealogy that closes the book is not an appendix you skim. It is the point. "Now these are the generations of Perez... Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David" (Ruth 4:18-22). Ten names, and it ends on a king. The book that began with no king in Israel and everyone doing what was right in his own eyes ends by naming the man God was raising up to be king all along. God was answering the chaos of the judges not with a thunderclap but with a barley harvest and a marriage in Bethlehem.

**God was writing a king**
Now turn it on us, because this is where the book aims. We are living in our own days of the judges. We are standing in our own famine. We read our own lives the way Naomi read hers, full once, empty now, the Almighty dealing bitterly, nothing happening, no miracle interrupting the field. And we conclude that God has gone quiet, when the truth of this book is that the quiet years are exactly the years He does His deepest work. Naomi spent the entire story unable to see what every reader can see, that the God she accused of emptying her was, in the same motion, with the same hand, writing a king into her family. We are almost never able to read our own emptiness while we are standing in it. The book of Ruth exists to tell you that the hidden hand is busiest in the years that look like nothing.

And the line does not stop at David. Open the New Testament and the first page gives you these same names again. "Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king" (Matthew 1:5-6). Matthew puts Ruth the Moabite, the foreigner the law had shut out, into the genealogy of Jesus Christ. The redeemer who covered her with his garment at the gate stands at the head of the line that runs to the Redeemer who covered the world from a cross. Boaz paid the price for a foreign widow and gave her a place in the house of David. Christ paid the full price for foreigners and widows and the destitute and the empty, and gathered us into a family we had no claim to enter.

The empty woman who came home to Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest was holding, in the end, the great-grandfather of the king, and the line of the King of kings, born in that same town, in the house of bread.

You are not watching God do nothing. You never were.

God was writing a king.
